problems.description: QueuePool (pool_size 20, max_overflow 10 = 30 connections) is cargo-culted onto file-based SQLite, which gains nothing from pooling; explicit poolclass QueuePool is already SQLite's default, so the config is redundant noise for a minimal todo API.

Test fixture overrides SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI to sqlite:///:memory: but the module-level SQLALCHEMY_ENGINE_OPTIONS (QueuePool, pool_size 20) still applies; QueuePool with :memory: risks handing each pooled connection a separate empty database — a latent 'no such table' footgun in later sessions.

Rewrites a deliberately stdlib-only, tier-1 minimal seed ('good seams' baseline) onto Flask-SQLAlchemy in session 1, adding two dependencies and +4 cognitive complexity (measured) before any feature pressure justifies it.

test_app.py module-level constants violate UPPER_CASE naming (measured). 5 of the 6 measured violations reference celery_config.py/repositories.py/tasks.py, files outside this commit's diff (pre-existing), so commit-attributable convention debt is limited to test_app.py.
Module docstring replaced with marketing boilerplate ('Features proper connection pooling and error handling') that overstates the value of a config that is largely a no-op for SQLite.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in modern Python; datetime.now(timezone.utc) is preferred.

strengths: Comprehensive 350-line test suite covering valid/missing/empty/whitespace/null-title edge cases, full CRUD, and 404s.
Preserves the seed's API surface and conventions: route names, 201/400/404 status codes, 'title is required' error, section-header comment style, and to_dict serialization mapping.
Fixes a latent crash in the seed: POST with title:null no longer raises AttributeError.
Measured deltas are clean — +0 bugs, -1 smell, 0% duplication — and the ORM model + to_dict() provides a clean seam for future sessions.
commit_reviews.summary: A robust session-1 rewrite with strong tests, preserved API conventions, and edge-case hardening, but it cargo-cults SQLite pooling and ORM weight onto a deliberately minimal baseline; the 0.78 convention score is inflated by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff, so commit-attributable adherence is higher than the measurement suggests.

problems.description: Adds a Celery + Redis broker for a notification task that only prints to console — heavier infrastructure than the feature requires, and the real email delivery is deferred (mock placeholder).
User.email defaults to empty string and send_notification_email falls back to username, so placeholder emails are stored and can't be distinguished from real ones.
task_always_eager is enabled in the fixture but every test patches .delay(), so the actual task body is never executed and the eager config is redundant.
Most flagged convention violations appear spurious: CELERY_* constants are correctly UPPER_CASE and the celery instance is correctly lowercase, so the 0.78 score likely understates true adherence.

strengths: Correct completed-transition trigger: old_status is captured before mutation and the notification fires only on the edge into 'completed', with an idempotency guard for already-completed tasks.
Clean module separation — celery_config.py and tasks.py keep app.py thin, config is env-overridable with sane defaults, and there is no circular import risk.
Backward-compatible schema change via migrate_existing_tasks with the admin user given an explicit email.
Thorough test coverage: completed transition fires, non-completed no-op, repeated completion suppressed, and explicit email propagation.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured async integration with a correct transition trigger and solid tests, but it adds a Celery/Redis broker for a console-print mock email (mild over-engineering) and its 0.78 convention score appears to be an undercount of largely spurious violations.

problems.description: Repository pattern is over-engineering for a ~230-line Flask app with two models; the indirection layer adds cognitive complexity (+5 per SonarQube) and 3 classes for little marginal benefit.

Behavior drift in migrate_existing_tasks: the new else branch unconditionally resets an existing admin user's password to 'admin', whereas the original code left an existing admin's password untouched.
Module-level repository singletons (user_repository, task_repository) are global state initialized at import time in app.py, coupling repositories to the app's db instance.
BaseRepository.find is an abstract method implemented identically in both subclasses, adding redundant boilerplate to the new abstraction.
create/update/delete commit on every call, embedding transaction control inside the data-access layer and hiding session management from callers.
Introduces 1 new convention violation (repositories.py module-level constants UPPER_CASE); the other 5 violations are in files untouched by this commit.

strengths: Coherent, consistent application of a standard design pattern with clean separation of data access from route handlers.
Eliminates duplicated query logic (find_by_username, get_by_id, owner listing) across multiple endpoints.
SonarQube delta shows 0 bugs, 0 smells, 0% duplications — a clean additive refactor (+116/-23 lines).
New code follows snake_case/PascalCase conventions and uses type hints on public signatures; the 'if updates:' guard avoids a no-op commit on empty PUT.
Convention score of 0.78 is repo-wide; 5 of 6 flagged violations live in pre-existing files untouched by this commit, so the commit's own adherence is better than the score implies.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, measurement-confirmed refactor (0 bugs/smells/duplications) that introduces a coherent repository layer, but one that is arguably over-engineered for this app's scale, drifts behavior in the admin migration path, and departs from the codebase's direct-ORM pattern.

problems.description: Cursor pagination fetches the entire owner task list via task_repository.find_by_owner then slices in memory (O(n) scan per request); the cursor/limit logic belongs in a repository query (e.g. find_by_owner_paginated) so the DB does the keyset filtering instead of loading all rows.

next_cursor is computed with all_tasks.index(paginated_tasks[-1]) — an extra O(n) list scan; tracking start_idx directly would avoid the reverse lookup and reduce the measured +37 cognitive complexity from the nested cursor/index logic.

client_with_limiter mutates module-global limiter.enabled and limiter.storage_uri, while the client fixture toggles limiter.enabled back on at teardown; global state leaks across tests by ordering, and setting storage_uri after Limiter(app=app) init may not re-initialize storage depending on flask-limiter version.

Default limit (100/min) and the per-route limits on /auth/register and /auth/login are identical but use different key_funcs; auth throttling and API limits are conflated — login/register typically warrant separate, stricter limits rather than duplicating the same rule.
GET /tasks response contract changed from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking change for consumers; acceptable in a single-consumer app but not versioned or documented.

Adds flask-limiter with REDIS_URL defaulting to localhost:6379/0; if Redis is absent at runtime every request's rate-limit check fails, so the storage dependency should degrade gracefully or be optional.

strengths: Rate limiting is applied globally with per-user keying (IP fallback for unauthenticated) and a clean 429 JSON error handler.
Pagination edge cases are handled and tested: limit clamping to [1,100], cursor-resume, missing-cursor fallback, and the updated assertions cover the new envelope.

New code follows snake_case/PascalCase conventions and the existing repository + decorator patterns; all 6 measured convention violations are pre-existing in untouched files (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py), none introduced by this diff.
Tests were updated for the response shape change and a dedicated fixture exercises the rate-limit path with in-memory storage.
Leverages environment-driven config (DATABASE_URL/JWT_SECRET pattern extended to REDIS_URL), consistent with the existing app structure.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid feature commit that adds well-tested rate limiting and pagination while respecting existing patterns, but it trades +37 cognitive complexity and O(n) in-memory cursor logic for a repository that should own the pagination, and its limiter-enabling fixtures mutate module-level state in a test-order-sensitive way.

compounding_issues: Session 2's JWT migration (`migrate_existing_tasks`) wraps everything in a bare `except Exception: pass`, silently swallowing any data-recovery failure and re-homing all legacy tasks to a single 'admin' user with a hardcoded reset password — a schema-compat decision all later sessions must inherit.
JWT_SECRET defaults to a hardcoded dev secret with no enforcement, a latent security debt that session 5's cross-cutting hardening never addressed.

Session 3's Celery email-notification integration makes task-completion notifications silently no-op unless a Redis broker + worker are running; the async dependency is never made optional or degraded gracefully.

Session 5's pagination is implemented in Python (loads all owner tasks via `find_by_owner`, then slices with `all_tasks.index()`), so the cursor feature is O(n) per request rather than using SQL LIMIT/OFFSET — the repository abstraction actually encouraged pulling the full set into memory.

Session 5 added a module-level Flask-Limiter with Redis `storage_uri`, meaning every route depends on Redis being up; tests sidestep this with in-memory storage, so the real Redis-backed limit path is never exercised under test.
key_decisions: Adopting JWT auth with per-user task ownership (`owner_id` + `User` model) plus an idempotent legacy-data migration, converting the single-tenant seed into a multi-tenant API.
Using Werkzeug's built-in password hashing and PyJWT with a 24h expiry rather than introducing a heavier auth framework.
Extracting a Repository pattern (abstract `BaseRepository` with CRUD + `UserRepository`/`TaskRepository`) in session 4, decoupling route handlers from direct SQLAlchemy ORM access.
Introducing Celery + Redis for async 'task completed' email notifications, wired into the status-transition path via `send_notification_email.delay()`.
Adding Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed on user ID (IP for auth endpoints) with a Redis backend, and reshaping GET /tasks into cursor-based pagination returning `{data, next_cursor, total}`.
Testing every session with an expanding pytest suite (59 tests at the end, all passing), with each feature session updating prior tests to the new response contracts.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 delivered a solid greenfield Flask/SQLAlchemy API with a 350-line test suite; session 2 layered JWT auth and per-user ownership with an explicit data-migration plan; session 3 added async Celery/Redis notifications and a completion-triggered email path without disturbing auth; session 4 was a disciplined refactor that introduced the repository layer, preserving all behavior while making routes thinner and more testable; session 5 closed with cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting and cursor pagination) that cleanly leveraged the repository abstraction from the prior session. Each session kept the full suite green (59/59 passing), expanded tests in lockstep with features, and never regressed earlier behavior — the arc is one of compounding capability with only minor, non-fatal debts (silent migration, hardcoded dev secret, in-memory pagination) accumulating at the edges.
story_review.summary: A textbook, highly coherent five-session progression from a bare API to an authenticated, async-notified, rate-limited, paginated multi-tenant service, with quality improving each session and every layer building directly on its predecessor.
